doc.title: Frank Foster — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Tenor models: Dexter Gordon, Wardell Gray and Sonny Stitt
summary: On tenor he followed Gordon and above all Sonny Stitt, whom he calls clear and predictable but derivative of Bird.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: As soon as I switched to tenor, then here comes Dexter Gordon and -- not so much Wardell [Gray] -- Sonny Stitt. Wardell was a minor influence. I later played with Wardell in person. In my own young immature mind, I thought I blew him away. So Sonny Stitt was my next step and Dexter Gordon. Dexter Gordon then Sonny Stitt. Sonny Stitt was the ultimate.
So when I made the switch, Sonny Stitt was the first one that really influenced me.
Was this via records, or did you have encounters with Stitt?

Records only. Every note was crystal clear. None of the notes slid into each other so, that a phrase became indistinct. When Sonny Stitt [Foster sings a bop melody], everything was right there where it needed to be. Everything, as I said, was crystal clear. No doubt, no hesitation, no, “What was that? Was that” --
Well how different at that point was Stitt from Bird?
Not that different. I mean Bird -- I guess Bird was able to elude me with some of his phrases.
You think Stitt was a little bit more predictable?
Yes, okay. Stitt was a bit more predictable, but I didn’t fault him for that predictability. If I knew where he was going, I wanted to go there in the first place.
It seems to me that the facility was there the same as Bird or maybe not that much difference.
But maybe something in the spark of the idea, in the melodic things he would create. There’s still some slight separation between what Bird left us and what Stitt left us.
I think Bird was the more creative, more imaginative.
The more seminal. I think Bird was more the source and Sonny Stitt was more derivative but captivating in his style.
